title: Why Creek Oxygen Rises and Falls

scenes.tts: In the tank, oxygen rose by day and fell at night. Why? Picture a whole creek sharing the two jobs from the first film. Keep the same colors while the view pulls back into moving water.
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's color map exactly: photosynthesis green; respiration red; oxygen and water blue; light and energy yellow; carbon dioxide and labels grey. Begin inside the familiar leaf cell, then pull back through a leaf into a creek cross-section. Blue water flows slowly while the question fills the open sky area.
scenes.narration: In the tank, oxygen rose by day and fell at night. Why? Picture a whole creek sharing the two jobs from the first film. Keep the same colors while the view pulls back into moving water.

scenes.visual: Keep the creek water, plants, and drifting particles moving. Show the title 'Why Creek Oxygen Rises and Falls' for two seconds, then shrink it beside the time bar.

scenes.tts: Green algae and underwater grass fill the sunlit creek. Fish, tiny animals, and microbes drift nearby. A blue gauge tracks dissolved oxygen, the oxygen gas mixed into water. A time bar begins at sunrise.
scenes.visual: Fill the frame with one creek cross-section. Place green algae and grass below, small fish and animal icons midwater, and grey microbe dots near all organisms. Build a large blue dissolved-oxygen gauge at right and label it 'schematic'. Start a yellow-to-dark time bar at sunrise across the top.
scenes.narration: Green algae and underwater grass fill the sunlit creek. Fish, tiny animals, and microbes drift nearby. A blue gauge tracks dissolved oxygen, the oxygen gas mixed into water. A time bar begins at sunrise.

scenes.tts: Yellow sunlight reaches the algae and grass. These producers make food by photosynthesis. Their photosynthesis sends blue oxygen bubbles into the water. At the same time, red respiration arrows pull oxygen toward living things. Both processes are running.
scenes.visual: Sweep yellow rays onto algae and grass. Grow green arrows that release blue oxygen bubbles. At the same time, draw red arrows carrying blue bubbles toward grass, algae, fish, and microbes. Keep both arrow systems moving on the same creek picture.
scenes.narration: Yellow sunlight reaches the algae and grass. These producers make food by photosynthesis. Their photosynthesis sends blue oxygen bubbles into the water. At the same time, red respiration arrows pull oxygen toward living things. Both processes are running.

scenes.tts: Watch the arrows, not just the bubbles. A rate tells how fast a process runs. The photosynthesis arrow grows wider than the respiration arrow. Oxygen enters the water faster than living things use it. The blue gauge climbs, and the schematic line rises.
scenes.visual: Combine all green additions into one wide green rate arrow and all red uses into one narrower red rate arrow. Raise the blue gauge. Draw a blue line upward beside the time bar and label it 'schematic'. Animate every new point from the arrow-width difference.
scenes.narration: Watch the arrows, not just the bubbles. A rate tells how fast a process runs. The photosynthesis arrow grows wider than the respiration arrow. Oxygen enters the water faster than living things use it. The blue gauge climbs, and the schematic line rises.

scenes.tts: The grass and algae appear beside animals on the respiration side. Plants do not stop respiring when they photosynthesize. Their cells also need usable energy. During daylight, whether oxygen rises or falls depends on which rate is faster.
scenes.visual: Slide grass and algae icons onto the red respiration side beside fish and microbes, while their green photosynthesis arrows remain active. Pulse small yellow usable-energy marks inside every organism. Balance the green and red rate arrows like opposing flows into the blue gauge.
scenes.narration: The grass and algae appear beside animals on the respiration side. Plants do not stop respiring when they photosynthesize. Their cells also need usable energy. During daylight, whether oxygen rises or falls depends on which rate is faster.

scenes.tts: The time bar reaches sunset. The yellow light fades, so photosynthesis stops adding new oxygen. Respiration keeps using oxygen. If nothing else changes, what should the blue line do next?
scenes.visual: Move the time marker to sunset. Fade the yellow rays and narrow the green addition arrow to zero. Keep the red use arrow moving. Stop the schematic blue line exactly at sunset and show the question beside its unfinished night section.
scenes.narration: The time bar reaches sunset. The yellow light fades, so photosynthesis stops adding new oxygen. Respiration keeps using oxygen. If nothing else changes, what should the blue line do next?

scenes.visual: Hold the unfinished blue line and question. Keep water particles drifting, organisms moving gently, and the red respiration arrow flowing. Do not extend the line during the thinking pause.

scenes.tts: The line bends downward through the night. Fish, plants, and microbes keep respiring in darkness. The oxygen gauge falls because living things keep using oxygen and photosynthesis no longer replaces it. Photosynthesis adds oxygen in light; respiration uses oxygen day and night. At sunrise, light can turn the green addition back on.
scenes.visual: Extend the schematic blue line downward across the dark time bar. Lower the blue gauge while the red arrows keep carrying oxygen to all organisms. At the far edge, let a yellow sunrise begin and a thin green arrow start growing again.
scenes.narration: The line bends downward through the night. Fish, plants, and microbes keep respiring in darkness. The oxygen gauge falls because living things keep using oxygen and photosynthesis no longer replaces it. Photosynthesis adds oxygen in light; respiration uses oxygen day and night. At sunrise, light can turn the green addition back on.

scenes.tts: Transform the creek gauge into a bathtub level. Photosynthesis is a tap controlled by light. Respiration is a drain that stays open. When the tap outruns the drain, the level rises. With the tap off, it falls.
scenes.visual: Morph the blue oxygen gauge into a large bathtub without cutting away. Transform the green addition arrow into a tap linked to the day-night bar. Transform the red use arrow into an open drain. Raise and lower the water level as the relative arrow widths change.
scenes.narration: Transform the creek gauge into a bathtub level. Photosynthesis is a tap controlled by light. Respiration is a drain that stays open. When the tap outruns the drain, the level rises. With the tap off, it falls.

scenes.tts: Now transform the tub back into the creek. Make both rate arrows equal, and the gauge holds steady. Widen photosynthesis, and the gauge rises. Widen respiration, and it falls. Whether the level rises or falls follows the difference between the rates.
scenes.visual: Morph the tub back into the same creek cross-section. Set the green and red rate arrows to equal widths while the schematic gauge holds. Widen the green arrow and raise the gauge. Then widen the red arrow and lower it. Keep the time bar and organisms moving gently.
scenes.narration: Now transform the tub back into the creek. Make both rate arrows equal, and the gauge holds steady. Widen photosynthesis, and the gauge rises. Widen respiration, and it falls. Whether the level rises or falls follows the difference between the rates.

scenes.tts: The smooth line is a model, not a promise about every hour. A real sensor may not follow it exactly. Use the model to ask which process pushes oxygen up or down. Then investigate other causes separately.
scenes.visual: Keep the smooth blue line labelled 'schematic'. Place a faint question mark beyond it rather than drawing a real record. Pulse the green addition arrow when 'up' is spoken and the red use arrow when 'down' is spoken. Leave open space beside the creek for later causes.
scenes.narration: The smooth line is a model, not a promise about every hour. A real sensor may not follow it exactly. Use the model to ask which process pushes oxygen up or down. Then investigate other causes separately.

scenes.tts: Compare the green addition with the red use before judging the line. In light, both arrows run. In darkness, the use continues without the addition.
scenes.visual: Return to the full creek. Place green addition and red use arrows beside the schematic blue gauge, with one grey question mark for other causes. Then transform the green and red arrows into the exact end-card sentence while all other objects fade.
scenes.narration: Compare the green addition with the red use before judging the line. In light, both arrows run. In darkness, the use continues without the addition.

scenes.visual: Show one line only, centered at large size: 'Photosynthesis adds oxygen in light; respiration uses oxygen day and night.' No title, subtitle, icon, or smaller line.
